guides.title: Hierarchy
guides.what: Calculate a compactification scale and Higgs mass for a chosen SU(7) bulk content, and compare the moment approximation with the implemented full Fourier potential.
steps: Start with a Table 1 row so the selected matter content has a named reference.
Read the gauge-seed choice before comparing any numbers. Changing it changes the potential.
Compare the approximate and full-potential minima, masses and scales. Then change one multiplicity and repeat.
Open the approximation and uncertainty diagnostics; use their own coupling and W-mass conventions when reading their results.
guides.read: A ceiling here belongs to its stated moment approximation, seed, coupling and mass window. A numerical result, an interval certificate for a fixed potential and agreement with a published physical model are different claims. The published-phase discrepancy remains open.
guides.purpose: Use this tool to see how changing bulk matter changes the scale associated with an extra dimension. A smaller nonzero Wilson phase can correspond to a larger compactification scale. The tool lets you compare an inexpensive small-angle approximation with calculations of the same implemented potential. Begin with the named examples; only interpret a changed model after checking which assumptions you changed.

controls.name: Bulk multiplicities
controls.meaning: Counts of the eight supported representation/parity types. These are discrete choices of matter content, not measured probabilities.
controls.try: Load one published row, then change one count by one.

controls.name: Gauge seed
controls.meaning: Selects the printed gauge weights or the candidate split. The seed changes the Fourier coefficients and the arithmetic conditions.
controls.try: Repeat the same content under both choices and retain the seed in any comparison.

controls.name: Published rows and pre-registered sixth row
controls.meaning: Load explicitly recorded contents. A row is a reproducible input, not a promise that its printed phase will be reproduced.
controls.try: Read the printed value and the laboratory value side by side.

controls.name: Robustness: g₄, model span and winding cutoff
controls.meaning: Separate a coupling scenario from numerical convergence. Increasing the number of Fourier terms tests truncation; a coupling span is an assumed model range.
controls.try: Change the cutoff while holding the physical inputs fixed, then vary the coupling separately.

outputs.name: Wilson phase, Higgs mass and compactification scale
outputs.meaning: Read which potential and convention produced each value. Compare the approximate and full-Fourier columns at matching inputs, with GeV and TeV kept distinct.

outputs.name: Distance to a ceiling
outputs.meaning: A conditional bound for the stated approximation. It is not automatically an attainable content or a bound for every full-potential vacuum.

outputs.name: Uncertainty budget and experimental references
outputs.meaning: Numerical bounds, recorded W-mass input uncertainty, coupling scenarios and unquantified physical effects have separate meanings. The ATLAS and CMS Higgs-mass entries are separate comparisons.

example.title: Compare an approximation with its full potential
steps: Load a Table 1 row and leave the seed unchanged.
Record the approximate phase, Higgs mass and scale.
Open the moment/full-Fourier comparison and read the differences and available bounds.
Increase the Fourier cutoff in the diagnostic and compare again without changing g₄.
example.expect: You can distinguish a truncation effect from an approximation error. Agreement between these calculations does not resolve the physical gauge-determinant question.

formulas.meaning: The scale conversion in this SU(7) convention, for a nonzero phase. The factor belongs to this convention; do not transfer it unchanged to a different model's phase variable.

limits: The physical choice of gauge determinant still requires reconciliation with the literature. The eight reconstructed fermion tables do not settle that separate issue.
The small-angle moment approximation has a domain of validity. Check its error against the full potential before using a derived mass or ceiling.
Higher-loop and other physical theory uncertainties are not quantified by a Fourier-tail bound. The displayed uncertainty components are not a complete statistical confidence interval.

troubleshooting.symptom: The scale is absent or an output is declined.
troubleshooting.action: Check for a symmetric or flat potential and for a zero phase. Read the stated reason rather than replacing a missing value with zero.

troubleshooting.symptom: Two panels give different masses.
troubleshooting.action: Compare their seed, potential, coupling, W-mass anchor and approximation labels before comparing their digits.

guides.title: Design a scale
guides.what: Search for integer bulk contents compatible with a target compactification scale and Higgs-mass window under the displayed SU(7) moment conventions.
steps: Choose the gauge seed and enter the target scale and Higgs-mass window in the displayed units.
Run the design search or inspect a rung separately.
Read the named outcome and its assumptions. A budget stop leaves the question undecided.
Load a returned content into the model and check its full potential in Hierarchy before using it.
guides.read: The search works on an arithmetic reduction of the model. An impossibility certificate is limited to the problem it states; a found content still needs its potential and vacuum checked. A stopped search supplies neither existence nor impossibility.
guides.purpose: Use this when you have a desired scale and want to know whether the allowed integer matter choices can reach it. The reachable-set plot explains why a continuous target slider does not imply a continuous family of available theories. Some gaps can be certified arithmetically; other searches end because their computational budget is exhausted.

controls.name: Target 1/R₅ and Higgs-mass window
controls.meaning: Define the requested region in the displayed scale and mass units. These are design assumptions; entering them does not turn them into experimental constraints.
controls.try: Start from the prefilled target, then make a small change and compare the selected lattice points.

controls.name: Rung buttons and lattice-point probe
controls.meaning: Restrict the arithmetic problem to one rung or point so you can inspect its obstruction or construction.
controls.try: Compare a successful point with a neighbouring refused point.

controls.name: Require W > 0
controls.meaning: Applies the named preliminary screen before the full potential is asked. Passing this screen does not certify a global minimum.
controls.try: Read the screen explanation before enabling it in a search.

controls.name: Design and Load into the model
controls.meaning: Run the bounded search, then transfer a returned content into the laboratory's SU(7) model.
controls.try: Keep the search outcome and inspect the transferred content in Hierarchy.

outputs.name: Reachable-set clusters
outputs.meaning: Resolve a cluster into individual allowed points before interpreting its width as a continuous interval.

outputs.name: floor, cone, congruence, dual or exhaustion
outputs.meaning: Different reasons the specified arithmetic problem has no solution: a lower bound, a cone restriction, a modular condition, a separating rational certificate, or completed enumeration. Read the accompanying certificate.

outputs.name: budget
outputs.meaning: The permitted work ended before the question was decided. This is an incomplete search outcome.

example.title: Follow a design through to a physical calculation
steps: Run the prefilled design problem.
If a content is returned, save its input values and use Load into the model.
Open Hierarchy with the same seed and compare the approximate and full-potential outputs.
If the search instead stops, read whether it supplied a certificate or only a budget message.
example.expect: The search and the potential check answer successive questions. A lattice solution alone is not a certificate of a physically viable model.

limits: Bounds and impossibility statements inherit the seed, mass window, coupling convention and arithmetic reduction used by the search.
A positive preliminary screen does not establish a global vacuum or agreement with experimental data.
The reachable set shown is for the stated search problem; changing the model family requires a new problem.

troubleshooting.symptom: The target lies between displayed points.
troubleshooting.action: Expand the cluster into its individual points and inspect the certified gap before increasing a search budget.

troubleshooting.symptom: The search reports budget.
troubleshooting.action: Reduce the requested region or use the rung/point controls to isolate the question. Keep the result labelled undecided.

guides.title: Count a rung
guides.what: Count supported SU(7) bulk contents at selected moment coordinates without having to list every content individually.
steps: Let the initial table finish, then read the selected gauge seed and coordinate range.
Move the A₄ probe on the graph and compare counts across the displayed rungs.
Use the extended range only when you need it; it increases memory use.
Keep published-seed and candidate-seed counts separate when comparing results.
guides.read: A count records distinct input contents in the stated arithmetic fibre. It does not count physically inequivalent theories or certify acceptable full-potential vacua. Archived enumeration totals validate specific counting cases.
guides.purpose: Use this to understand how many discrete matter choices share a moment condition, especially when direct enumeration becomes expensive. A large count can reveal a large family of inputs, but many inputs may share the same potential or fail a later physical check. Compare this page with Same potential? to understand those different notions of sameness.

controls.name: Gauge seed
controls.meaning: Changes the admissible rungs and moment lattice. The candidate case has even rungs and half-integral A₄ coordinates.
controls.try: Inspect the labels and counts after a seed change rather than reusing a previous row.

controls.name: A₄ graph probe
controls.meaning: Chooses a moment coordinate where the counting function is evaluated.
controls.try: Move between neighbouring displayed points and read the integer counts.

controls.name: Extended range / rebuild
controls.meaning: Recomputes the counting table over the chosen range. The extended range is a larger memory task.
controls.try: First understand a small-range result, then extend it if needed.

outputs.name: Counts by rung
outputs.meaning: The number of supported nonnegative integer contents satisfying the selected moment conditions.

outputs.name: Counting-function graph
outputs.meaning: Shows how the count changes with the moment coordinate. A large value is a combinatorial multiplicity, not a probability.

outputs.name: Archived enumeration comparisons
outputs.meaning: Specific independent totals against which the counting method has been checked. They do not certify every physical interpretation of a counted input.

example.title: See why many inputs can share one coarse description
steps: Start with the default counting range.
Select a point with several contributing contents and note its rung and A₄ coordinate.
Move one coordinate step and compare the count.
Open Same potential? to see why equality of a few moments is weaker than equality of the full potential.
example.expect: The counts are discrete and coordinate-dependent. They describe an arithmetic fibre, not a histogram of observed particles.

limits: The measured-mass fibre recorded for the published seed is not transferred automatically to the candidate seed.
Counts do not impose all phenomenological requirements, anomaly completion or full-potential vacuum tests.
A content count and an equivalence-class count answer different questions.

troubleshooting.symptom: The graph changes substantially after switching seed.
troubleshooting.action: Read the new rung and coordinate conventions; the admissible lattice itself has changed.

troubleshooting.symptom: The extended table is slow or uses substantial memory.
troubleshooting.action: Return to the ordinary range and use a smaller question. A resource limit should not be interpreted as a zero count.

references.label: Part VIII: counting and the inverse problem

guides.title: Atlas
guides.what: Browse the 1,286 supported SU(7) bulk contents with at most five multiplets, compare their potential shapes and load an example into the model.
steps: Draw the lattice and wait for the tiles to finish.
Read the colour legend and the selected seed before comparing tiles.
Hover over a tile to inspect its content; select it to see the details.
Use Load into the model to investigate the selected content in the other SU(7) tools.
guides.read: Each tile is a content in a finite catalogue. Its colour summarizes the displayed calculation under its conventions. A flat-potential tile is a mathematical outcome, not missing experimental data; a favourable colour is not a complete model-validation claim.
guides.purpose: Use the atlas when you want a visual starting point instead of choosing eight multiplicities from scratch. It shows how different input contents lead to different potential shapes within a small, completely specified catalogue. A useful workflow is to notice an interesting tile, load it, and then inspect its approximation error, anomaly content and source comparison.

controls.name: Draw the whole lattice
controls.meaning: Calculates and displays the finite catalogue. Let the calculation finish before treating an incomplete display as the full set.
controls.try: Start once and read the legend while the tiles populate.

controls.name: Tile selection
controls.meaning: Identifies one discrete bulk content and its displayed verdict.
controls.try: Compare a flat tile with one that has a nonzero minimum.

controls.name: Load into the model
controls.meaning: Transfers the selected content to the shared SU(7) model used by the neighbouring tools.
controls.try: Open Hierarchy immediately after loading and check that the multiplicities match.

outputs.name: Potential tiles
outputs.meaning: Small plots ordered by the calculated phase. Read the numerical details before comparing shapes at different scales.

outputs.name: Content and verdict
outputs.meaning: The supported representation/parity counts and the result of the stated mass-window calculation.

outputs.name: Flat potentials
outputs.meaning: Contents whose implemented potential has no phase-dependent preference at the displayed order. A unique broken vacuum cannot be inferred from a flat curve.

example.title: Turn a visual candidate into an inspectable model
steps: Draw the atlas with the default conventions.
Select the tile corresponding to a named published row and inspect its content.
Load it into the model and open Hierarchy.
Compare the mass-window verdict with the full-potential and uncertainty diagnostics.
example.expect: The same input content can be followed from a thumbnail to a detailed calculation. The catalogue's size limit remains part of what was searched.

limits: The catalogue stops at five multiplets; it is not an enumeration of every possible bulk content.
A plotted minimum or mass-window colour is not a proof of anomaly cancellation, a complete flavour sector or experimental viability.
The SU(7) normalization and literature-discrepancy cautions also apply to these tiles.

troubleshooting.symptom: A tile appears blank or flat.
troubleshooting.action: Inspect its content and flat-potential classification before assuming a drawing failure.

troubleshooting.symptom: The loaded model seems different from another comparison.
troubleshooting.action: Check its gauge seed and every multiplicity; a tile label alone does not specify a different panel's coupling or approximation settings.

references.label: Part VII: SU(7) potential and finite catalogue

guides.title: Same potential?
guides.what: Compare two SU(7) bulk contents using the full-potential coordinates, and distinguish equal potentials from equal low-order moments.
steps: Use the shared model as content A and copy it into content B.
Apply a displayed kernel relation or edit B's multiplicities.
Read the five-coordinate comparison as well as the curves.
Load the equal-moment example to see how matching local moments can leave different full potentials.
guides.read: For the stated potential family, equality of the five coordinates is the algebraic equality criterion. Two overlapping plots alone cannot prove an identity. Matching only the selected local moments is weaker and can leave different global behaviour.
guides.purpose: Use this to avoid counting different matter descriptions as different one-loop potentials. It also demonstrates a common limitation of approximations: two models can agree on the few coefficients used near a symmetric point while differing elsewhere. The algebraic comparison and the numerical graph are deliberately shown together so you can tell an identity from a visually small difference.

controls.name: Content B: copy, clear and multiplicities
controls.meaning: Creates the second input independently of the shared content A.
controls.try: Copy A first so the initial equality has an obvious cause.

controls.name: Kernel-relation arrows
controls.meaning: Rewrite a content using a relation that leaves the potential coordinates unchanged, subject to valid nonnegative counts.
controls.try: Apply an available arrow and inspect which multiplicities change.

controls.name: Canonical of A
controls.meaning: Chooses the canonical representative used by the implemented algebraic reduction.
controls.try: Compare its content with A while keeping the coordinates in view.

controls.name: Equal-moment example and plot range
controls.meaning: Loads a pair with matching selected local moments and lets you compare local and full phase ranges.
controls.try: Read the small-angle view, then expand to the full range.

outputs.name: Five potential coordinates
outputs.meaning: The complete identity test for this stated family. Equality has a stronger meaning than agreement at sampled plot points.

outputs.name: Two potential curves
outputs.meaning: A numerical illustration of the algebraic comparison. Use the full range to inspect structure hidden by a local zoom.

outputs.name: Moment diagnostics and evidence
outputs.meaning: Show which selected moments coincide and what the available exact or interval checks establish about the example.

example.title: Compare exact equality with approximate agreement
steps: Copy A to B and verify coordinate equality.
Apply a permitted kernel relation; the content changes while the identity criterion remains satisfied.
Load the equal-moment example.
Compare the local and full plots and read the separate full-potential conclusion.
example.expect: A kernel rewrite and a low-order moment match have different logical strength. Use the coordinate or certificate statement, not the apparent thickness of an overlaid curve.

limits: The equality criterion concerns the implemented one-loop potential family and its conventions. It does not prove that all particle spectra, couplings or boundary sectors are identical.
Numerical agreement at finitely many phase values does not establish an analytic identity.
A canonical representative of a potential is not automatically a canonical representative of the complete physical theory.

troubleshooting.symptom: A relation arrow cannot be used.
troubleshooting.action: Check whether the proposed rewrite would require a negative multiplicity.

troubleshooting.symptom: The curves look identical but the tool distinguishes them.
troubleshooting.action: Read the exact coordinate comparison and use the full phase range; a plot may hide a small or distant difference.

references.label: Part VII: potential coordinates and kernel relations

guides.title: Anomalies & proton
guides.what: Inspect the SU(7) bulk anomaly contributions and the boundary matter needed to cancel them; the separate RS experiment studies another model's anomaly flow.
steps: Load a named SU(7) content in Hierarchy and return here.
Read the signed contributions to 8D and the six anomaly channels.
Check the selected seed before interpreting the displayed rung ladder.
Follow the brane-matter construction in Escape, or open the separate RS anomaly-flow experiment for its own inputs and assumptions.
guides.read: A nonzero bulk anomaly contribution is an obligation for the complete model to cancel. It is not by itself a final inconsistency verdict when boundary matter is allowed. A forbidden arithmetic rung is a statement under the selected seed's assumptions.
guides.purpose: Use this to connect a compact anomaly number with the fields that contribute to it. The signed bars help you see why adding a multiplet can increase or decrease the total. The brane construction then asks whether additional boundary matter can cancel the relevant channels while meeting a separate proton-protection condition.

controls.name: Shared SU(7) bulk model
controls.meaning: Supplies the matter multiplicities used by the bars and channel table. Edit it in Hierarchy or load a named row.
controls.try: Compare two published rows and track which contributions change.

controls.name: Gauge seed and rung information
controls.meaning: State the arithmetic convention behind the ladder and the conditional ceiling.
controls.try: Read the rung parity after changing seed; do not carry a previous impossibility statement across the change.

controls.name: RS anomaly-flow shortcut
controls.meaning: Opens an embedded warped-model experiment with its own parameters and outputs.
controls.try: Use its dedicated guide before comparing UV and IR contributions.

outputs.name: Signed contribution bars
outputs.meaning: Show how individual multiplets contribute to the displayed anomaly combination, in the stated eighth-unit normalization.

outputs.name: Six-channel table
outputs.meaning: Separates the anomaly conditions that a proposed matter completion must satisfy. Cancellation in one combination is not cancellation in every channel.

outputs.name: Rung ladder and brane-construction costs
outputs.meaning: Relate the arithmetic of the selected bulk content to the boundary assignments examined by the laboratory.

example.title: Trace an anomaly total back to its content
steps: Load a published SU(7) row in Hierarchy.
Read its total and individual bars on this page.
Change one bulk multiplicity in Hierarchy and return.
Open Escape to inspect all channels for an explicit boundary assignment.
example.expect: The total is connected to individual contributions, while the completion must be checked channel by channel.

limits: Bulk-only anomaly information does not describe every possible boundary completion.
An anomaly cancellation calculation does not determine a proton lifetime.
The RS anomaly-flow experiment is a separate model. Its UV/IR results are not corrections to the SU(7) table.

troubleshooting.symptom: A nonzero row seems to contradict a usable model.
troubleshooting.action: Check which fields are included. The bulk subtotal and the complete bulk-plus-boundary ledger answer different questions.

troubleshooting.symptom: The ladder interpretation changes with the seed.
troubleshooting.action: Read the seed-dependent arithmetic statement and compare only calculations made under matching assumptions.

references.label: Part VI: anomaly and boundary-matter construction

guides.title: Escape from proton decay
guides.what: Construct the supported SU(7) boundary-matter assignments and check their anomaly cancellation and proton-protection selection rules separately.
steps: Start with a listed assignment so its rung and charge conventions are explicit.
Change the rung choices, X_Q or q_φ one at a time.
Read every anomaly channel, then the allowed-operator and residual-symmetry information.
Compare the result with the selected bulk model's required anomaly cancellation.
guides.read: Cancellation and operator protection are separate tests within the implemented assignment family. A protected operator pattern is not a calculated proton lifetime, and enumerating this family does not classify every possible completion.
guides.purpose: Use this when you want to see how a boundary completion can cancel the bulk contribution while restricting dangerous operators. The tool makes the charges and assignments explicit so that a successful label can be traced back to a concrete choice.

controls.name: Rung choices
controls.meaning: Select the boundary assignment in the displayed charge lattice.
controls.try: Load one of the twenty listed assignments before editing its rungs.

controls.name: X_Q and q_φ
controls.meaning: Charge parameters entering the anomaly conditions and the selection rule. Use the exact rational conventions shown by the panel.
controls.try: Change one charge and compare the anomaly table with the operator verdict.

controls.name: Rung cube
controls.meaning: A view of the assignment space and where the protection condition changes.
controls.try: Rotate it, then select a listed assignment to inspect its numbers.

outputs.name: Six anomaly channels
outputs.meaning: Exact rational contributions for the supported content. Check every channel rather than only a displayed total.

outputs.name: Selection rule and residual group
outputs.meaning: Identify which supported operators the charge assignment permits or forbids.

outputs.name: Boundary contribution against the bulk
outputs.meaning: Shows whether this completion supplies the cancellation required by the current bulk input.

example.title: Separate cancellation from protection
steps: Load a listed assignment and record both verdicts.
Change a rung or charge.
Read which channel or operator condition changed.
Restore the assignment and verify that the original two conclusions return.
example.expect: You can explain a verdict from the charge and channel tables rather than relying on its colour.

limits: The enumeration concerns the implemented assignment family and operator tests.
No proton decay rate, hadronic matrix element or experimental lifetime likelihood is evaluated here.
A complete model may need additional matter and interaction checks beyond these conditions.

troubleshooting.symptom: Cancellation succeeds but protection changes.
troubleshooting.action: Read the operator selection rule separately; an anomaly condition does not determine every allowed interaction.

troubleshooting.symptom: The boundary contribution does not match the bulk.
troubleshooting.action: Confirm the selected SU(7) content and seed, then compare channel signs and charge normalization.

references.label: Part VI: boundary assignments and operator protection

guides.title: Multiplets & parities
guides.what: Inspect how supported SU(7) representations split under the boundary symmetries, and how their parity signs determine zero modes and potential terms.
steps: Choose a supported representation and read its parity labels.
Use the cube and the component table together to identify which fields occupy each corner.
Read the derived fermion term table and its comparison with the reference coefficients.
Keep the gauge-sector split and its unresolved physical interpretation separate from the reconstructed fermion tables.
guides.read: A zero mode is a component allowed by the displayed boundary conditions. Reconstructing fermion coefficients checks that part of the potential; it does not determine the complete physical gauge determinant.
guides.purpose: Use this to connect the representation names in the bulk-content editor with the components that survive the boundaries. The cube is a visual index of signs; the component and coefficient tables contain the detailed information.

controls.name: Representation selector
controls.meaning: Chooses the supported multiplet whose decomposition is displayed.
controls.try: Start with the fundamental representation, then compare a tensor representation.

controls.name: Parity and intrinsic-sign choices
controls.meaning: Specify how a component transforms at the boundaries and which sign enters its Fourier term.
controls.try: Change one available sign and follow the affected components.

controls.name: Parity cube
controls.meaning: Groups components by their displayed Z₂ signs.
controls.try: Rotate it and read the table instead of inferring multiplicity from a drawing alone.

outputs.name: Component decomposition
outputs.meaning: The subgroup representations and parity assignments obtained from the supported parent representation.

outputs.name: Zero-mode information
outputs.meaning: Identifies components allowed to remain massless by the stated boundary projection before additional mass-generating effects.

outputs.name: Derived term table
outputs.meaning: Checks the Fourier coefficients reconstructed from the component signs against the implemented reference.

example.title: Follow one sign through the calculation
steps: Select the fundamental representation.
Read a component's boundary signs and zero-mode label.
Change an available intrinsic sign.
Compare the component and Fourier-term tables before and after.
example.expect: You can identify which boundary choice changes a component or a potential contribution, without treating the sign cube as a spectrum calculation by itself.

formulas.meaning: The sign product shown for this potential convention. Read the definitions of the component and intrinsic signs on the panel.

limits: Only the supported representation and boundary conventions are covered.
Boundary-allowed zero modes can be lifted by interactions that are outside this decomposition.
The eight fermion tables and the physical gauge-sector question have different evidence status.

troubleshooting.symptom: A component exists in the decomposition but has no zero mode.
troubleshooting.action: Check its individual boundary parities; belonging to the parent representation is not sufficient to survive the projection.

guides.title: Screen a table
guides.what: Arithmetic screens for a published row, with conditional rung certificates and independent full-potential witness checks.
steps: Type the row's two observables.
Read the mod-6 law, the K invariant and the arithmetic comb.
Open Conditional rung bounds and check the seed, coupling and Higgs-mass window before using a ceiling.
Compare the archived full-Fourier witnesses: a stationary point may have a deeper competing vacuum.
guides.read: The interval certificates bound a small-angle moment relaxation under the stated conventions. They do not certify a ceiling for the full potential. The separate vacuum checks compare numerically located extrema with Fourier-tail errors; an observed surviving witness is not an exhaustive optimum.
guides.purpose: Use this to check whether a proposed SU(7) row is compatible with the implemented arithmetic before doing a broader calculation. It also provides access to the certificate dossier. Read which question each certificate answers: a fixed-potential global minimum and a conditional ceiling for a moment relaxation are different mathematical statements.

controls.name: Row inputs
controls.meaning: The observables or arithmetic quantities labelled by the screen. Preserve the source's units and rounding when entering a printed row.
controls.try: Load a listed row before typing an alternative.

controls.name: Gauge seed, coupling and mass window
controls.meaning: The conventions conditioning the arithmetic and bound comparisons.
controls.try: Read them beside a certificate before comparing its ceiling with another result.

controls.name: Save certificate buttons
controls.meaning: Download the archived evidence, assumptions and associated checks as JSON.
controls.try: Save a bundle when recording a result so its scope travels with the number.

outputs.name: Arithmetic laws and K invariant
outputs.meaning: Consistency screens within the stated model reduction. A failed screen identifies the stated mismatch; a passed screen leaves later tests open.

outputs.name: KK comb
outputs.meaning: The allowed arithmetic spacing displayed in squared mass. It should not be read as equally spaced masses.

outputs.name: Formal and interval evidence
outputs.meaning: The dossier distinguishes exact algebra, certificates for ten fixed one-phase potentials, conditional moment ceilings and separate numerical witness comparisons.

example.title: Read a certificate without enlarging its claim
steps: Load one archived row and read all three screens.
Open the conditional bound information and record the seed and mass window.
Compare a full-potential witness with one labelled as having a deeper competing vacuum.
Save the evidence bundle and follow the attribution link.
example.expect: A stationary point can pass one test while failing the global-vacuum comparison. The exported assumptions explain which conclusion can be reused.

limits: A moment-relaxation ceiling is not a universal ceiling for full-potential vacua.
Numerically checked witnesses do not establish exhaustive optimality.
Mathematical certificates for the implemented potential do not resolve the outstanding physical gauge-determinant choice or establish scientific novelty.

troubleshooting.symptom: A printed row fails a screen.
troubleshooting.action: Check rounding intervals, units and seed first, then read the specific failed relation. Do not infer that an entire paper is wrong from one mismatch.

troubleshooting.symptom: A stationary witness has a lower competing vacuum.
troubleshooting.action: Keep the stationarity result but withdraw the claim that this witness is the global vacuum.

guides.title: Collider
guides.what: Which state a dijet search bounds, plus a separate Higgs-rate scenario checked against pinned experimental datasets.
steps: Use the Higgs-rates shortcut to compare a saved scalar scenario, its widths and rates, and matching HiggsBounds/HiggsSignals calculations.
Read the coupling and invisible-width assumptions alongside the HiggsSignals chi-square and the analysis selected by HiggsBounds.
Read the coloron's mass and width — both fixed by the localisation, not chosen.
Drag the relief over (M_jj, χ), the plane CMS bins its angular measurement in.
Type any 1/R₅ to see the ratio table move.
guides.read: The dijet Δχ² values are quoted from the published record; the Higgs experiment computes its own comparison. Its 159 HiggsSignals observables are not 159 independent degrees of freedom. Coupling and width assumptions can compensate in visible rates, so this scalar comparison is not a complete GHU fit.
guides.purpose: Use this to connect a model's coloured state with the particular dijet measurement used in the archived comparison. The separate Higgs-rates experiment studies a specified scalar-coupling scenario. Keeping those two subjects distinct prevents a limit on one particle hypothesis from becoming an unsupported verdict about a whole GHU model.

controls.name: Compactification scale 1/R₅
controls.meaning: Sets the model scale for the displayed colour-sector comparison.
controls.try: Change it and read the model-to-reference ratios at the named bins.

controls.name: Dijet relief
controls.meaning: Displays the predicted distortion over the dijet mass and angular variable used in the measurement.
controls.try: Rotate the view and read the axes and reference-bin labels.

controls.name: Higgs-rates shortcut
controls.meaning: Opens the separate coupling/width experiment and its matching experimental calculations.
controls.try: Start with its Standard Model reference before changing a coupling.

outputs.name: Coloron mass, width and coupling
outputs.meaning: Belong to the stated localization and colour-sector assumptions; they are not freely interchangeable with another resonance model's parameters.

outputs.name: Dijet ratio and archived Δχ²
outputs.meaning: The displayed comparison retains the provenance of the original recast. It is not a newly executed fit to every dataset stored in the laboratory.

outputs.name: CMS reference snapshot
outputs.meaning: Seven distributions and 77 bins are archived with source records. The correlation table concerns fitted signal strengths and is not an unfolded-spectrum covariance matrix.

example.title: Inspect the hypothesis behind a collider comparison
steps: Read which coloured state and localization assumptions define the current calculation.
Record the scale and one named-bin ratio.
Change the scale while retaining the particle hypothesis.
Open the dataset/source description and distinguish the archived recast from newly stored reference data.
example.expect: The numerical response is traceable to a named hypothesis and analysis. Importing a dataset alone has not created a new GHU exclusion.

limits: A published bound is reusable only to the extent that its production, decay and acceptance assumptions match the proposed state.
The stored CMS data have not been combined into a new laboratory likelihood or a new GHU fit.
The HiggsTools comparison belongs to its supplied scalar scenario. Its observable count is not automatically the statistical number of degrees of freedom.

troubleshooting.symptom: A limit seems much stronger than another panel's limit.

troubleshooting.action: Use a matching saved reference, import a matching result or explicitly run the configured local engine. Do not reuse a result for different couplings.

guides.title: Selection rule
guides.what: Check the supported SU(4) representation and Wilson-domain selection conditions, including the chiral-count test for a quark-generation embedding.
steps: Select the Dynkin labels (a, b, c), which identify the representation.
Read the centre-charge condition and the permitted Wilson-line search domain.
Inspect all three embedding conditions before using the displayed count.
Compare a passing representation with one that fails a single condition.
guides.read: The count applies under the displayed projection and embedding conditions. Classical centre-charge facts and the series' chiral-count calculation have separate attribution. Passing these representation tests does not construct a complete quark sector.
guides.purpose: Use this before choosing a representation or reducing a vacuum-search domain. Boundary symmetries can relate some phase values, but the allowed reduction depends on the content. The embedding test asks a second question: whether the supported representation can contain the required chiral structure under the stated projection.

controls.name: Dynkin labels a, b, c
controls.meaning: Nonnegative integer labels of an SU(4) representation; changing them changes the representation, not a continuous coupling.
controls.try: Start with a catalogue entry and change one label.

controls.name: Test the rule on every representation
controls.meaning: Runs the displayed finite catalogue comparison.
controls.try: Read the tested range together with the verdict.

controls.name: Shared SU(4) content
controls.meaning: Connects the selection rule to the matter content used by the calculator.
controls.try: Inspect the domain again after editing that content.

outputs.meaning: The domain justified by the selected content's symmetry. An unjustified reduction can miss a vacuum.

outputs.name: Three embedding conditions
outputs.meaning: Centre-charge parity, a nonzero middle Dynkin label and the stated size condition must be read together.

outputs.name: Chiral count
outputs.meaning: The count for the stated projection when its hypotheses hold; it does not specify Yukawa couplings or measured quark masses.

example.title: Check a proposed representation before calculating its vacuum
steps: Choose a catalogue representation.
Record each condition and the permitted domain.
Change one Dynkin label and inspect which condition changes.
Follow the representation to Model calculator using a domain justified for that content.
example.expect: You can distinguish a representation-selection result from the later potential and mass calculations.

formulas.meaning: The displayed count under the panel's three embedding conditions and chiral projection. The symbol here is a count, not the SU(4) gauge-group rank.

limits: The conditions use this SU(4) embedding and boundary projection; they are not a universal criterion for every GHU model.
A finite catalogue check does not replace the stated proof assumptions.
An allowed representation does not settle masses, interactions or anomaly completion.

troubleshooting.symptom: The count is unavailable or a condition fails.
troubleshooting.action: Read the failed condition before interpreting the formula. Do not evaluate an out-of-scope count as an accepted embedding.

guides.title: Model calculator
guides.what: Evaluate the supported SU(4) one-loop potential, locate its vacuum and calculate the associated Higgs curvature for a chosen matter content.

Set multiplicities, boundary signs and the displayed matter/gauge roles.
Read the vacuum location and the reference-reproduction indicator.
Use Selection rule to understand the search domain, and eta-meter to inspect sign sensitivity.
guides.read: Mass ratios remove some overall normalization dependence but retain the model and approximation assumptions. Absolute masses and scales require the stated normalization and physical inputs. The anchor indicator tests a named reference calculation, not general phenomenological validity.
guides.purpose: Use this as the numerical workspace for the SU(4) model family. Loading the published reference gives you a reproducible starting point. You can then change one representation count or sign and see how the vacuum and mass response change.

controls.name: Load AHMN / clear

controls.try: Record the anchor before making any changes.

controls.name: Representation multiplicities
controls.meaning: Add or remove copies of supported representations from the catalogue.
controls.try: Change one count by one and compare the vacuum.

controls.try: Keep a record of these labels with the multiplicities; the counts alone are insufficient.

controls.try: Use the justified domain rather than choosing the smaller search only for speed.

example.title: Measure one change relative to the anchor
steps: Load AHMN and note the vacuum and mass ratio.
Change one multiplicity while keeping its sign and role fixed.
Read the new vacuum and potential cut.
Reload AHMN and confirm the baseline is restored.
example.expect: The difference is attributable to one documented input change. A successful reference reproduction is a check on that calculation.

A mass ratio can remain sensitive to content, vacuum selection and approximation even when an overall normalization cancels.
The finite representation catalogue is the implemented search range.

troubleshooting.symptom: A reduced search gives another minimum.

guides.title: eta-meter
guides.what: Compare the analytic and directly evaluated response of supported SU(4) multiplets to their boundary sign η.
steps: Choose a multiplet or load the AHMN content.
Compare the predicted sign response with the directly evaluated Hessian.
Draw the atlas and select η-difference mode to isolate the sign-dependent part.
Filter sign-sensitive and insensitive multiplets, then compare individual tiles.
guides.read: Insensitivity to η concerns the specified difference or contribution. It does not mean that a representation contributes nothing to the potential or has no physical effects. The analytic statement and the finite numerical checks have their stated scope.
guides.purpose: Use this to understand why changing a boundary sign sometimes moves a result and sometimes leaves it unchanged. Difference mode removes the common part of two calculations, making an otherwise hidden dependence easier to see.

controls.name: Multiplet and content choices
controls.meaning: Choose the contribution or combined content being studied.
controls.try: Compare one sensitive multiplet with one labelled insensitive.

controls.name: Flip every η
controls.meaning: Changes the selected boundary signs together while retaining the content.
controls.try: Read the predicted response before applying the flip.

controls.name: Potential / η-difference
controls.meaning: Switches between the full landscape and the difference under sign reversal.
controls.try: Use both views for an insensitive multiplet.

controls.name: Atlas filters and two-tile comparison
controls.meaning: Select the displayed subset and compare two contributions at matching conventions.
controls.try: Keep the display mode unchanged while switching tiles.

outputs.name: Predicted versus evaluated response
outputs.meaning: Compares the closed-form calculation with the direct numerical calculation of the stated quantity.

outputs.name: Difference landscape
outputs.meaning: A zero difference indicates sign insensitivity in that calculation, even if the full potential is nonzero.

outputs.name: Finite catalogue check
outputs.meaning: Tests the implemented rule across the 119 supported representations.

example.title: See what a zero difference means
steps: Choose a multiplet labelled insensitive to η.
Inspect its full potential.
Switch to η-difference mode and read the zero response.
Choose a sensitive multiplet and compare the same two views.
example.expect: A vanishing difference and a vanishing potential are visibly different statements.

limits: The result concerns the specified SU(4) sign dependence and projection.
Numerical comparisons retain their cutoff and precision assumptions.
Sign insensitivity alone does not determine the full spectrum or phenomenological viability.

troubleshooting.symptom: An atlas tile becomes blank in difference mode.
troubleshooting.action: Check whether it is classified as sign-insensitive; a zero difference can be the expected result.

guides.title: Five dimensions
guides.what: Evaluate the supported Haba–Yamashita five-dimensional SU(3) example and compare its potential, located vacuum and Kaluza–Klein spectrum.
steps: Load the archived row, then identify the six matter counts and their parity-product signs.
Compare the evaluated potential with its located minimum and the separate approximation when available.
Use the pure-gauge, marginal-trio and blind-step examples to change one structural feature at a time.
Read the spectrum at the resulting phase and retain this model's normalization conventions.
guides.read: This is a particular 5D model family. Its even-rung arithmetic and phase normalization should not be replaced by those of the 6D SU(7) family. The located vacuum and a small-angle approximation must be compared within their domains.
guides.purpose: Use this compact example to learn how matter and boundary signs shape a Wilson-line potential. The six counts separate the supported adjoint fermion, fundamental fermion and scalar contributions by parity-product sign. The preset buttons supply controlled comparisons without requiring a new model from scratch.

controls.name: Adjoint fermion counts, + and −
controls.meaning: Numbers of the supported adjoint Dirac fields in the two parity-product sectors.
controls.try: Start from the archived row and change one count.

controls.name: Fundamental fermion and scalar counts, + and −
controls.meaning: Separate fermionic and complex-scalar contributions; their signs and degrees of freedom enter the potential differently.
controls.try: Use the blind-step button to inspect the specific cancelling combination.

controls.name: Archived row / pure gauge / marginal trio
controls.meaning: Load the named reference or a targeted example with stated matter content.
controls.try: Compare pure gauge with the marginal trio while reading the potential and moment diagnostics.

outputs.name: Evaluated potential and minimum
outputs.meaning: The phase dependence of the implemented source formula and the minimum located for that input.

outputs.name: Moment/rung diagnostics
outputs.meaning: Describe the arithmetic of this supported five-dimensional content, including its even-rung property.

outputs.name: KK spectrum
outputs.meaning: The tower structure at the selected vacuum under this model's boundary and normalization conventions.

example.title: Separate a content change from a potential change
steps: Load the archived row and note its potential.
Apply the blind-step example.
Check the changed counts and compare the potential.
Use the marginal-trio example and inspect the changed vacuum behaviour.
example.expect: Different matter counts can have the same implemented potential contribution. The preset states which combination is being tested.

limits: The page covers the stated SU(3) family and supported matter sectors.
The 5D parity-product and phase conventions differ from those of the SU(7) family.
A one-loop vacuum and spectrum do not establish a complete phenomenological model.

troubleshooting.symptom: A content change leaves the curve unchanged.
troubleshooting.action: Check whether the change is the displayed blind combination of fermion and scalar contributions.

troubleshooting.symptom: The approximation is unavailable near a marginal case.
troubleshooting.action: Read the direct potential and the stated domain restriction instead of forcing a small-angle formula.

guides.title: SU(N) builder
guides.what: Build a supported five-dimensional SU(N) model on S¹/Z₂ from boundary blocks and bulk matter, then inspect its one-loop potential and vacuum.
steps: Start from a preset or enter the four nonnegative boundary-block sizes.
Add supported bulk representations, their parity-product signs and copy counts.
Read the resulting group and number of Wilson phases before interpreting the potential.
Follow the same model into 4D spectrum, Anomalies, Brane matter and Simulator.
guides.read: The builder covers the implemented boundary and representation families. A one-phase reduction permits additional moment diagnostics under their stated assumptions. A located vacuum may be undecided in a harder search; an unfinished calculation is not a proof that no vacuum exists.
guides.purpose: Use the builder as the starting point for a connected model investigation. The four blocks specify simultaneously diagonal boundary parities. Their sizes determine N and the apparent boundary-symmetry structure. The bulk fields supply the matter contributions to the potential. Neighbouring tools share this builder state, so you can inspect the spectrum and anomaly obligations without retyping the model.

controls.name: n₊₊, n₊₋, n₋₊, n₋₋
controls.meaning: Nonnegative dimensions of the four simultaneous parity blocks. Their sum fixes the SU(N) rank parameter.
controls.try: Load a preset first and identify which blocks are nonzero.

controls.name: Bulk representation, ηη′ and multiplicity
controls.meaning: Choose a supported field contribution, its boundary-sign product and the number of copies.
controls.try: Add one supported copy while keeping the boundary blocks fixed.

controls.name: Presets and clear bulk
controls.meaning: Provide named starting inputs or a gauge-only matter setting.
controls.try: Read a preset's boundary blocks before changing it.

controls.name: Potential probe
controls.meaning: Selects a phase at which to inspect the potential; the probe and the located vacuum are distinct positions.
controls.try: Click away from the minimum and compare the probe information with the vacuum result.

outputs.name: Apparent unbroken subgroup
outputs.meaning: The group visible in the chosen boundary frame. Its appearance need not be invariant under gauge-equivalent boundary descriptions.

outputs.name: Potential terms and Wilson phases
outputs.meaning: Show what the supported matter and boundary data contribute and how many independent phase directions are being investigated.

outputs.name: Vacuum result
outputs.meaning: A located minimum or a stated undecided/unsupported result under the numerical method's scope.

example.title: Carry one model through the laboratory
steps: Load a named builder preset.
Record its blocks and bulk content.
Open 4D spectrum and read its zero modes at the selected phase.
Open Anomalies, then Brane matter if a completion is needed.
Use Simulator for the model's dimensionful comparison.
example.expect: The same builder input is inspected from several perspectives. A favourable result in one view does not substitute for the others.

formulas.meaning: The boundary block dimensions add to the defining-representation dimension of SU(N).

limits: Supported representations and simultaneously diagonal parity blocks define the implemented model family; the builder does not represent every possible 5D theory.
A brane interaction or supersymmetric cancellation absent from the implemented potential cannot be inferred from the model name.
Minimum searches, moment approximations and global certificates have different scopes.

troubleshooting.symptom: There is no Wilson-line direction.
troubleshooting.action: Inspect the chosen boundary blocks and surviving gauge-field components; a valid boundary condition need not leave a Higgs candidate.

troubleshooting.symptom: The vacuum is labelled undecided.
troubleshooting.action: Retain that status and inspect the stated search limitation. Do not substitute a symmetric point as a certified minimum.

guides.title: Paper models
guides.what: Four models somebody else published, taken off their pages and run through this instrument's engine.
steps: Use the Maru–Nago shortcut for Type 2/3 SU(6), the magnified minimum and Fourier convergence; its button transfers the supported bulk potential to the builder.
Pick one of the four; Kubo–Lim–Yamashita carries a dial, the number of triplet fermions.
Read the table: what the paper prints, then what this returns, then the verdict.
Press Load into the SU(N) builder and walk the spectrum, the ledger and the simulator on their model.
guides.read: Three of the four are supersymmetric and this engine's potential is not, so their rows are boundary-condition and zero-mode statements only. An amber row disagrees with one printed equation, not with a paper, and names which of that paper's own equations agrees with which.
guides.purpose: Use this to begin from a named published construction and see which of its statements the laboratory can actually reproduce. The reference table separates boundary and zero-mode information from potential calculations. The Maru–Nago experiment is an additional supported SU(6) potential study with its own guide.

controls.name: Model selector
controls.meaning: Chooses one of the four archived model comparisons.
controls.try: Read the source and supported comparison scope immediately after selection.

controls.name: Triplet-fermion count, where available
controls.meaning: Changes the matter input in the Kubo–Lim–Yamashita example.
controls.try: Compare two counts while retaining the same boundary conditions.

controls.name: Load into the SU(N) builder
controls.meaning: Transfers the supported boundary and bulk input for further inspection.
controls.try: Open 4D spectrum after loading and compare the supported zero-mode statement.

controls.name: Maru–Nago shortcut
controls.meaning: Opens the separate Type 2 / Type 3 experiment.
controls.try: Read its convergence study before transferring its bulk potential.

outputs.name: Printed statement / computed result / verdict
outputs.meaning: Compares a specific source claim with the laboratory result and retains the source's equation or table reference.

outputs.name: Explanation rows
outputs.meaning: Describe normalization, implementation scope or disagreements that a short status label cannot explain.

outputs.name: Transferred model
outputs.meaning: Contains only the supported input; additional interactions of the original construction may remain outside the builder.

example.title: Reproduce one statement from a paper
steps: Select a published model and read its scope note.
Choose a boundary or zero-mode row with an explicit source reference.
Load the model into the builder and inspect the corresponding spectrum.
Read any discrepancy at the level of the named statement.
example.expect: You can trace one comparison from source to input to output without treating it as a reproduction of every part of the paper.

limits: Three archived models are supersymmetric while the builder potential is not; their stated comparisons are limited to supported boundary and zero-mode information.
A disagreement with one printed equation is not a blanket judgement about an entire paper.
Transferred bulk data do not automatically include brane interactions, supersymmetric cancellations or flavour completion.

troubleshooting.symptom: A comparison is amber or limited in scope.
troubleshooting.action: Read the explanatory row and the cited equation before changing a normalization to make numbers agree.

guides.title: 4D spectrum
guides.what: What the model on the builder CONTAINS: the four-dimensional fields and their Kaluza–Klein towers.
steps: Edit the model in SU(N) builder — this section shares it.
Choose at the vacuum or type a phase.
Read the massless content, then the families, then the exact tower and its landscape.
guides.read: The families are the potential's multiset and are right for it; at a broken vacuum they are wrong at the LOWEST level of the adjoint and the symmetric tensor, which is why the exact tower is a second table and not a repetition.
guides.purpose: Use this to identify the four-dimensional fields supplied by the builder model and how their higher Kaluza–Klein levels are organized. The tables distinguish a family description useful for the potential from the exact tower accounting needed at exceptional low levels.

controls.name: Shared builder model
controls.meaning: Determines the boundary blocks and bulk representations whose spectrum is displayed.
controls.try: Use the named SU(6) example, then inspect the same blocks in the builder.

controls.name: At the vacuum / phase probe
controls.meaning: Chooses whether to evaluate the spectrum at the located vacuum or at a manually selected phase.
controls.try: Compare a symmetric point with the available broken vacuum.

controls.name: Spectrum landscape
controls.meaning: A rotatable view of the calculated levels; the tables retain the detailed multiplicities and labels.
controls.try: Read the lowest levels in the exact table before relying on the picture.

outputs.name: Massless content and chirality
outputs.meaning: The surviving four-dimensional components under the selected boundary and phase conditions.

outputs.name: Tower families
outputs.meaning: A compact organization of spectral contributions useful for reconstructing the potential.

outputs.name: Exact low-level tower
outputs.meaning: Resolves low-level details that the potential-family multiset alone does not describe correctly for every representation at a broken vacuum.

example.title: Compare the symmetric point with the vacuum
steps: Load the supplied SU(6) example.
Inspect the massless content at the symmetric point.
Switch to the located vacuum if available.
Compare the lowest exact levels, multiplicities and chirality labels.
example.expect: A phase change can alter which states remain massless. The potential's term multiplicities are not a substitute for the exact lowest-level spectrum.

limits: The spectrum uses the supported builder model and its boundary conditions.
Additional boundary masses and interactions require the separate completion analysis.
A plotted tower does not establish experimental production or decay rates.

troubleshooting.symptom: The family and exact tables appear to disagree at the lowest level.
troubleshooting.action: Read the page's explanation of exceptional lowest modes, especially for adjoint and symmetric-tensor fields at a broken vacuum.

troubleshooting.symptom: At the vacuum is unavailable.
troubleshooting.action: Return to the builder and inspect whether a vacuum was located or left undecided.

guides.title: Anomalies
guides.what: What that content owes: every anomaly channel of the unbroken group, in exact rationals.
steps: Edit the model in SU(N) builder.
Read the channels: [SU(n)]³, U(1)×[SU(n)]², U(1)³, U(1)×[grav]².
Read the verdict: no subject, cancels, or owes.
guides.read: A non-zero row is a BILL, not an inconsistency: the brane fermions such a model needs pay into the same channels with the opposite sign. And a model with no massless fermion has nothing to cancel — that is `no subject`, not `cancels`.
guides.purpose: Use this after inspecting the builder spectrum. It sums the supported chiral massless content into the anomaly channels of the displayed unbroken group. Exact rational arithmetic makes a cancellation distinguishable from a small floating-point residual.

controls.name: Shared builder content
controls.meaning: Supplies the boundary conditions and matter being checked.
controls.try: Load the supplied SU(6) example and inspect its massless fermions before reading the ledger.

controls.name: Model and spectrum choices
controls.meaning: Determine which supported chiral fields are included in the stated ledger.
controls.try: Change one builder field, then compare the summands as well as the total.

outputs.name: SU(n)³ and mixed U(1) channels
outputs.meaning: Separate non-Abelian, mixed, Abelian and mixed gravitational anomaly combinations under the displayed normalization.

outputs.name: Summand table
outputs.meaning: Names the chiral fields contributing to each channel; it explains the total.

outputs.name: No subject / cancels / owes
outputs.meaning: Distinguishes absence of relevant massless fermions, cancellation of the stated ledger, and a nonzero contribution requiring a completion.

example.title: Read a cancellation claim from its ingredients
steps: Load the supplied example.
Check the list of massless chiral fermions.
Read every nonzero channel and its contributors.
Open Brane matter to inspect a possible completion.
example.expect: A zero obtained from an empty fermion list is identified separately from cancellation between nonzero contributions.

limits: The ledger concerns the stated included spectrum and channels. It does not automatically settle all consistency conditions of a higher-dimensional completion.
A nonzero bulk contribution may be cancelled by suitable boundary matter; this page alone does not provide that completion.
Anomaly cancellation is not an experimental acceptance test.

troubleshooting.symptom: The total is zero but the verdict says no subject.
troubleshooting.action: Inspect the fermion list. There may be no relevant massless chiral fields to test.

troubleshooting.symptom: A nonzero channel remains.
troubleshooting.action: Record its normalization and contributors before adding boundary matter; cancellation must be checked with matching conventions.

guides.title: Brane matter
guides.what: Who pays that bill, and what it costs: matter on the two fixed points, held at once to the anomaly ledger and to Part I's boundary-mass gate.
steps: Edit the model in SU(N) builder — or press the example to load Kawamura's SU(5).
Read the two branes first: they are different groups whenever the orbifold breaks anything.
Add fields with the + buttons, or pick a massless mode and let the partners panel say which representations contain its conjugate.
Press solve to get the local charges that cancel the linear channels.
guides.read: Two verdicts, kept apart on purpose: the bill before and after, and the massless count before and after. The same field can pay one and not the other, because the charge that cancels an anomaly is not in general the charge a mass term needs. The surviving count is a lower bound — the rank test assumes generic couplings.
guides.purpose: Use this to add explicit matter at the two orbifold endpoints and inspect two consequences: changes to the anomaly ledger and possible boundary masses for unwanted zero modes. The local groups at the two endpoints can differ, so a representation that is available at one boundary need not be available at the other.

controls.name: Builder model / Kawamura SU(5) example
controls.meaning: Sets the bulk model and its local boundary groups.
controls.try: Load the named example and read both boundary-group headings.

controls.name: Boundary fields and copy counts
controls.meaning: Add representations of the selected endpoint's local group.
controls.try: Use the partner suggestions for one massless mode before adding fields arbitrarily.

controls.name: Boundary charges and linear-channel solver
controls.meaning: Choose charges or solve the stated linear anomaly conditions. The remaining channels still need inspection.
controls.try: Compare the suggested charge with the charge required for a boundary mass.

controls.name: Clear / reset charges / return to builder model
controls.meaning: Restore a defined starting point for a controlled comparison.
controls.try: Save the current choices before resetting.

outputs.name: Anomaly ledger before and after
outputs.meaning: Shows what the added fields contribute in the same channel conventions.

outputs.name: Possible partners
outputs.meaning: Lists supported local representations that contain a conjugate partner for the selected mode.

outputs.name: Surviving massless content
outputs.meaning: The rank-based result assumes generic allowed couplings; the displayed surviving count is a lower bound under that assumption.

example.title: Check the cost of removing a zero mode
steps: Load Kawamura's SU(5) example.
Choose an unwanted massless mode and inspect its possible partners.
Add a suggested local representation.
Compare both the anomaly ledger and the boundary-mass condition, including its charge.
example.expect: A field that helps one requirement can leave another unresolved. Read the two outcomes independently.

limits: Solving the linear anomaly channels does not by itself solve every cubic condition.
Generic-coupling rank information does not specify actual numerical masses or a complete Yukawa sector.
Only the supported local representations and boundary-mass conditions are examined.

troubleshooting.symptom: The anomaly-solving charge does not permit the desired mass term.
troubleshooting.action: Keep both conditions explicit and try another supported completion; do not treat the two charge requirements as interchangeable.

troubleshooting.symptom: A representation introduces additional fields.
troubleshooting.action: Read its full local decomposition, then include those fields in the updated ledger and surviving-content count.

guides.what: Search a bounded set of supported 5D SU(N) boundary conditions and bulk contents through selected group, Higgs, chirality, anomaly and vacuum filters.

Run the sweep and read the stage-by-stage funnel.
Load a surviving hit into the builder and inspect its detailed spectrum, ledger and vacuum status.
guides.read: The headline distinguishes boundary descriptions from equivalence classes. A hit passes the filters that were actually requested, within the searched range. Undecided vacuum calculations remain separate from rejected models.
guides.purpose: Use this when a single-model investigation suggests a precise search question. The filters run from cheaper structural checks to more expensive vacuum calculations. Starting with a small range makes it easier to understand which requirement removes candidates before increasing the search size.

controls.meaning: Define the finite model space to be enumerated.
controls.try: Use a small case to understand the funnel before increasing the range.

controls.meaning: Specify which supported conditions a candidate must pass.
controls.try: Change one filter at a time so you can identify its effect on the count.

controls.meaning: Distinguishes no requirement, any supported doublet and a colour-singlet doublet.
controls.try: Read the colour condition explicitly before interpreting a Higgs-candidate count.

controls.name: Run and load hit
controls.meaning: Perform the bounded search and transfer one result into the builder.
controls.try: Inspect a hit individually after the sweep.

outputs.meaning: Reports how many candidates were considered and survived each requested stage.

outputs.name: Boundary conditions and theory classes
outputs.meaning: Separates multiple descriptions of an equivalent model from distinct classes under the implemented equivalence.

outputs.name: Rejected and undecided cases
outputs.meaning: A failed condition and a vacuum question left unresolved are different outcomes.

steps: Run a small sweep with a minimal set of filters.
Record the tested range and stage counts.
Add a colour-singlet Higgs requirement or another supported filter.
Compare the funnel and load one surviving hit.
example.expect: You can state which requirement was imposed and how many inputs it removed. The result remains bounded by the selected search space.

Equivalent boundary conditions must not be counted as unrelated theories.
Passing the available filters does not supply every interaction or experimental comparison of a complete model.

troubleshooting.action: Read the first stage that removes all candidates and the exact searched range before claiming nonexistence.

troubleshooting.symptom: The vacuum stage reports undecided cases.
troubleshooting.action: Keep them in the unresolved category and investigate selected cases individually.

guides.title: One model, every verdict
guides.what: Compare supported model diagnostics across gauge-equivalent boundary descriptions and identify which results remain unchanged in that comparison.
steps: Start from the model in SU(N) builder.
Select another member of its displayed equivalence class.
Read the theory, frame and declined tags with their explanations.
Run the separate separation test to ask whether an invariant diagnostic distinguishes different classes.
guides.read: Invariance across the tested equivalent descriptions and ability to distinguish different theories are separate properties. The tags report the performed comparison; they should not be extended into an untested classification theorem.
guides.purpose: Use this to avoid mistaking a convenient description of a model for an observable property of the theory. A group or spectrum read at a fixed symmetric point can move under an equivalent boundary description. The dossier recomputes its diagnostics to show which quantities survive that change and which questions cannot be answered by the available calculation.

controls.name: Shared builder model
controls.meaning: Defines the equivalence class and diagnostics being examined.
controls.try: Begin with a model having more than one displayed class member.

controls.name: Class-member selection
controls.meaning: Changes the boundary description within the displayed equivalence class.
controls.try: Compare the same row before and after changing member.

controls.name: Separation test
controls.meaning: Asks whether the measured invariant distinguishes the different tested classes.
controls.try: Run it after understanding why a row is invariant within one class.

outputs.name: Theory / frame / declined tags
outputs.meaning: Summarize invariance, dependence on the chosen description, or a reason the calculation cannot supply a verdict.

outputs.name: Symmetric-point and vacuum diagnostics
outputs.meaning: Show why the point at which a property is evaluated matters to its interpretation.

outputs.name: Separation results

Select another class member and compare the same rows.
Read the separation test before using an invariant as a unique model identifier.

guides.title: Simulator
guides.what: Choose among three distinct calculation modes: the 5D builder model, a top-KK Higgs-production reference, or the 4D neutrino-ring research model.
steps: Choose Model to calculate and read the mode's own guide.
Start from a named reference or the restored default before changing one input.
Read the result summary, units and assumptions together.
Use the visible experiment guides for thermal, flavour and decay questions, then save the inputs and results.
guides.read: These modes answer different model questions and keep separate input records. The laboratory computes model responses and compares named references; it does not generate collider events. A missing matching external calculation remains pending rather than being borrowed from another input point.
guides.purpose: Use this page as the entry point for calculated masses and experimental comparisons. First identify the model you want to study. The builder mode follows the shared SU(N) input; the Higgs-production mode isolates a top-KK contribution; the neutrino mode studies a separate four-dimensional construction. Thermal and flavour experiments have their own inputs even when they appear on the same page.

The thermal SU(3) benchmark is separate from the current SU(N) builder model and from the SU(7) mass certificates.
Inputs supplied to calibrate or reconstruct a model are not subsequently predictions of those same observables.

guides.title: Boundary conditions
guides.what: Group supported orbifold boundary conditions into equivalence classes and compare their apparent symmetries under the stated ordinary-boundary relation.
steps: Select an available orbifold and the gauge-group parameter N.
Choose a boundary condition and inspect the other members of its class.
Compare the apparent groups within that class.
Read the conditions on any vacuum-energy comparison before interpreting it.
guides.read: The class count is about the specified equivalence relation and orbifold. A boundary description's apparent unbroken group can change within one class. The S¹/Z₂ count must not be transferred to another orbifold.
guides.purpose: Use this to see why listing boundary conditions can overcount theories. The tool walks explicit classes so you can inspect both their size and the different descriptions they contain. It also shows why a group name read at a symmetric point need not identify the whole equivalence class.

controls.name: Orbifold selector
controls.meaning: Chooses the available geometry and its supported boundary-condition relation.
controls.try: Compare S¹/Z₂ with T²/Z₃ and read the changed count rule.

controls.name: N and boundary multiplicities
controls.meaning: Set the finite condition being classified within the selected family.
controls.try: Start at a small N and inspect a class with several members.

controls.name: Class-member and energy views
controls.meaning: Select equivalent descriptions and inspect the explicitly permitted energy comparisons.
controls.try: Read What cannot be compared before using an energy ranking.

steps: Choose S¹/Z₂ at a small N.
Select a class containing more than one condition.
Compare the apparent group of two members.
Open One model, every verdict to investigate which calculated quantities remain invariant.

Classifying boundaries does not complete the model's matter content or phenomenology.
Energy comparisons are meaningful only under the conditions stated by that panel.

troubleshooting.symptom: The apparent group changes within a class.
troubleshooting.action: Read it as a property of the selected boundary description and symmetric point, then inspect the invariant diagnostics separately.

guides.title: Classify an orbifold
guides.what: Derive supported orbifold classification data from an integer rotation matrix, then compare the SU, SO and Sp cases under the stated hypotheses.
steps: Start with a supplied rotation before entering your own integer matrix.
Check that the matrix passes the finite-order and cyclotomic tests.
Choose the group family and N, then read the signature, alphabet and count information.
Inspect a datum-lattice cell and its fibre before comparing the plan and relief views.
guides.read: A refused matrix lies outside the implemented theorem's hypotheses; refusal is not a class count of zero. The rotation-matrix dimension and the gauge-group parameter N are different inputs.
guides.purpose: Use this to investigate which building blocks and local labels are available for a supported orbifold rotation. The 'alphabet' is the list of representation building blocks; a 'fibre' collects conditions sharing the selected local data. The plan and relief offer two views of the same computed field.

controls.name: Rotation preset or integer matrix
controls.meaning: Defines the torus rotation. Custom matrices are supported up to the stated rank-eight limit and must satisfy the implemented hypotheses.
controls.try: Classify a supplied example before modifying an entry.

controls.name: SU(N), SO(N), Sp(N) and N
controls.meaning: Choose the gauge-group family and parameter whose classification data are displayed.
controls.try: Keep the rotation fixed while comparing the three real forms.

controls.meaning: Select local multiplicity data and inspect the corresponding conditions.
controls.try: Compare a cell's class information with the number of conditions in its fibre.

outputs.meaning: The rotation's local singularity orders and the supported building blocks with their weights.

outputs.meaning: Describe the computed classification problem and its stated growth properties.

outputs.name: Plan, relief and selected fibre
outputs.meaning: Visualize the same datum field and expose the detailed contents of a selected cell.

example.title: Change the group while retaining the geometry
steps: Load a supplied rotation and classify it.
Read the signature and alphabet.
Compare SU, SO and Sp at the selected N.
Inspect the reality-type information to understand why the alphabets differ.
example.expect: The geometry stays fixed while the representation constraints of the group family change.

limits: Infinite-order matrices and matrices outside the stated cyclotomic hypothesis are refused.
A supported classification result does not calculate a phenomenological vacuum or experimental spectrum.
Local-data equivalence and the completeness of a proposed move set are separate questions, explored in Name the relations.

troubleshooting.symptom: A custom matrix is refused.
troubleshooting.action: Check that it is square with integer entries, then read which finite-order or cyclotomic condition failed.

troubleshooting.symptom: A plotted cell has no conditions.
troubleshooting.action: Inspect the rank and local multiplicity constraints; a selected coordinate need not be realizable.
