guides.title: Name the relations
guides.what: Which equivalence relation on boundary conditions the literature already owns, and whether a proposed move set connects a class.
steps: Pick an orbifold and a move.
Read the attribution: whose relation this is and where.
Run the walk to see whether the moves actually connect the class.
guides.read: The local/global distinction is the one that gets misquoted, and the page carries it explicitly.
guides.purpose: Use this to identify the existing mathematics behind a boundary-condition relation and test a proposed rewrite. A valid individual move must preserve the required data. A set of valid moves can still be incomplete if it leaves a class split into disconnected pieces.

controls.name: Orbifold, group and N
controls.meaning: Choose the configuration whose relations are being inspected.
controls.try: Start with a supplied small case.

controls.name: Proposed relation and Judge it
controls.meaning: Checks the entered move against the stated preserved data.
controls.try: Read exactly which condition is tested before interpreting a successful verdict.

controls.name: Walk a class
controls.meaning: Explores reachability under the selected moves in the tested finite case.
controls.try: Compare the number reached with the size of the class.

outputs.name: Attribution
outputs.meaning: Names the existing configuration, relation or result and its source. A known mathematical identification should retain that credit.

outputs.name: Move validity
outputs.meaning: Reports whether the specified rewrite preserves the tested data.

outputs.name: Connectivity and structural diagnostics
outputs.meaning: Separate finite-class reachability from broader claims about generating relations or complete intersections.

example.title: Distinguish a valid move from a complete move set
steps: Choose a supplied small configuration.
Inspect a proposed relation and its preserved data.
Run the class walk with the selected moves.
Compare the reached component with the full class size and read the attribution.
example.expect: A move can be legitimate while its move set fails to reach the entire tested class.

limits: A finite connectivity experiment does not prove completeness at every rank.
Local and global equivalence statements must retain their different hypotheses.
A relation already identified in the literature should not be presented as a new discovery of the laboratory.

troubleshooting.symptom: A move is rejected.
troubleshooting.action: Read which datum it changes; increasing the walk budget cannot repair a move that violates the required invariant.

troubleshooting.symptom: A valid move set reaches only part of a class.
troubleshooting.action: Keep the incompleteness result for that case and inspect which additional relations are needed.

guides.title: Conjugate boundary conditions
guides.what: Compare conjugate boundary conditions on S¹/Z₂ under two explicit hypotheses about the allowed transformations at the endpoints.
steps: Choose N and a symmetric or antisymmetric twist at each endpoint.
For odd N, read why the antisymmetric choice is unavailable.
Compare the independent-endpoint and linked-transformation conclusions side by side.
Read the Wilson-line and unbroken-group diagnostics with the hypothesis attached.
guides.read: Independent endpoint transformations give four classes at even N and one at odd N in the displayed classification. Linked transformations retain continuous information. The laboratory keeps these hypotheses explicit instead of treating one as an unconditional physical answer.
guides.purpose: Use this to understand why conjugate boundary conditions require a different classification from ordinary linear twists. They transform by congruence, and the allowed relation between endpoint transformations changes which information can be removed.

controls.name: N
controls.meaning: The gauge-group parameter; its parity affects which twist types exist.
controls.try: Compare a small even N with a small odd N.

controls.name: Twist at y = 0 and y = πR
controls.meaning: Choose a symmetric or, when allowed, antisymmetric conjugate twist at each endpoint.
controls.try: Inspect all allowed combinations at even N.

controls.name: Hypothesis comparison and Wilson-line card
controls.meaning: Show the consequences of independent versus linked endpoint transformations and the additional dimension-count diagnostic.
controls.try: Read the hypothesis before quoting a class count.

outputs.name: Counts under explicit hypotheses
outputs.meaning: A discrete classification under one assumption and retained continuous data under the other are different answers to different problems.

outputs.name: Wilson-line diagnostic
outputs.meaning: Examines the stated degrees of freedom; it does not silently transfer the ordinary-boundary conclusion.

outputs.name: Unbroken-group information
outputs.meaning: Must be interpreted with the selected twist and transformation hypothesis, not from a short label alone.

example.title: See why the hypothesis must accompany the count
steps: Choose an even N and inspect the allowed endpoint types.
Read both hypothesis columns.
Switch to an odd N and observe the unavailable antisymmetric choice.
Save a result with the hypothesis retained in its description.
example.expect: You can state precisely which classification problem produced a number.

limits: The calculation does not choose the correct transformation hypothesis for every physical construction.
Ordinary-boundary class counts do not automatically extend to antilinear twists.
The displayed structural diagnostic is not a full vacuum or phenomenological analysis.

troubleshooting.symptom: The antisymmetric option is refused at odd N.
troubleshooting.action: This is the stated existence condition, not a missing interface feature.

troubleshooting.symptom: Two columns give different kinds of answers.
troubleshooting.action: Compare the permitted endpoint transformations; the columns intentionally describe different equivalence hypotheses.

guides.title: Brane kinetic terms
guides.what: What happens to the tower when brane-localised kinetic terms make the masses stop being n/R.
steps: Use the Warped SU(6) shortcut to compare C1/C2 differential running, required UV brane terms and the separate localization probe.
Set the brane coefficient.
Read the roots of the transcendental mass equation.
Take the coefficient to zero and watch the ordinary twisted tower come back.
guides.read: The special functions are checked against mpmath at forty digits, and the c → 0 limit is computed in closed form by code that shares nothing with the solver. That limit found three real defects.
guides.purpose: Use this to see how kinetic terms localized at a boundary change a Kaluza–Klein mass equation and its roots. The zero-boundary-coefficient limit provides a useful check against a simpler tower. The warped SU(6) running card is a separate experiment and has its own inputs and guide.

controls.name: Brane coefficient c
controls.meaning: Controls the boundary kinetic contribution in the displayed mass equation.
controls.try: Compare a nonzero value with c = 0.

controls.name: α₁ and α₂
controls.meaning: The displayed phase parameters of this spectral example; retain its normalization when comparing another model.
controls.try: Vary one phase while holding c fixed.

controls.name: m and q
controls.meaning: The additional mass/charge parameters defined by the equation on the page.
controls.try: Read their role in the equation before changing both together.

controls.name: Demonstration / Warped SU(6) shortcut
controls.meaning: Run the guided spectral example or open the separate differential-running experiment.
controls.try: Use the demonstration first to connect the equation with its root plot.

outputs.name: Mass-equation roots
outputs.meaning: The allowed levels of the stated boundary problem; they need not be integer-spaced.

outputs.name: Tower view
outputs.meaning: Displays the same roots as a spectrum rather than as intersections of the mass equation.

outputs.name: Zero-coefficient comparison
outputs.meaning: Checks the solver against the ordinary twisted-tower limit under the same parameters.

example.title: Recover a known limit
steps: Run the supplied demonstration.
Record a few roots at nonzero c.
Bring c to zero while keeping the phases fixed.
Compare the resulting tower with the displayed closed-form limit.
example.expect: The numerical spectrum connects continuously to the stated reference limit where that limit applies.

limits: This is the supported spectral boundary problem, not a complete scan of all boundary operators.
A solver check does not establish every physical consistency property of an arbitrary kinetic-term choice.
The warped SU(6) running experiment is not a result computed from these spectral controls.

troubleshooting.symptom: The tower is no longer equally spaced.
troubleshooting.action: Read the modified mass equation; the boundary kinetic term changes the root condition.

troubleshooting.symptom: Two cases have different limits.
troubleshooting.action: Compare phases, m, q and normalization as well as the coefficient c.

guides.title: Gravity–gauge · 3D
guides.what: Which physical information a complete tower of masses leaves undetermined in a controlled gravity-gauge example.
steps: Start with p=1.1 and press eta=-0.9, eta=0, then eta=4. The paired masses stay equal while the Wilson scale and the response change.

Drag either 3D plot to turn it. On the response surface, switch drag to select point to change eta and the source position together. Shift-drag always turns; the wheel changes relief; arrow keys turn a focused plot.
Read the table below the plots. Choose gauge kinetic Z as the height to inspect the action. Use the header card or LaTeX buttons to export this exact input, or link to restore it.
guides.read: The positive paired tensor NN and vector DD masses are protected by their common canonical operator. The gauge NN control has different boundaries and moves. The source position is in the extra dimension, not a laboratory location; the Wilson kinetic scale is not a Higgs mass. For p=1.1 a canonical bulk scalar realizes the family, with stability and cutoff still open.
guides.purpose: Use this controlled example to distinguish knowing an entire sequence of masses from knowing how a source couples to those states. The paired mass towers can stay fixed while source residues and the Wilson kinetic scale change. The second, unprotected gauge tower provides a comparison with different boundary conditions.

controls.name: Geometry p
controls.meaning: Selects the displayed background; p = 1.1 is the scalar-supported example and p = 1 the AdS reference.
controls.try: Begin at p = 1.1.

controls.name: η and log₁₀(1 + η)
controls.meaning: Two ways to select the positive gauge-kinetic family parameter in its supported range.
controls.try: Compare the η = −0.9, 0 and 4 presets.

controls.name: Source t
controls.meaning: A position along the extra dimension, not a location in a laboratory detector.
controls.try: Move the source while comparing spectral weight with mass.

controls.name: Height, drag mode and 3D controls
controls.meaning: Choose spectral-weight ratio or Z(t); drag to rotate or select a point. Shift-drag rotates, the wheel changes relief, and focused plots accept arrow keys.
controls.try: Select a point on the response surface, then read its exact table values.

outputs.name: Paired tensor NN and vector DD masses
outputs.meaning: The protected comparison governed by the shared canonical operator and stated boundary conditions.

outputs.name: Vector NN control
outputs.meaning: Uses different boundary conditions and need not keep the same masses.

outputs.name: Response and Wilson kinetic scale
outputs.meaning: Additional information that is not fixed by the paired masses alone; the Wilson kinetic scale is not a Higgs mass.

example.title: Hold the paired masses while changing the response
steps: Set p = 1.1.
Compare η = −0.9, 0 and 4 at a fixed source position.
Read the paired masses and the response table at each setting.
Move the source and save a card or permalink for the selected point.
example.expect: The protected paired towers remain equal within the implemented construction while other response information changes.

limits: The boundary-condition pairing is essential; it does not protect every tower.
The construction does not calculate a Higgs mass, radion stability or collider rate.
Stability and cutoff questions remain open for the displayed family.

troubleshooting.symptom: Dragging changes the view instead of the selected parameter.
troubleshooting.action: Switch drag mode to select point; use Shift-drag when you want to rotate.

troubleshooting.symptom: The gauge control masses move while the paired masses do not.
troubleshooting.action: Check the boundary labels. The NN control is deliberately outside the protected NN/DD pairing.

Automated text signals help locate possible subjects, while curated entries name the page or equation behind an interpreted claim. The distinction matters when deciding whether a paper actually reports the quantities needed for a comparison.

Read which comparison quantities are actually supplied.
Keep keyword-only or unopened entries separate in your notes.

guides.title: Simulator: 5D builder predictions

It translates the dimensionless model into quantities that can be compared with measurements, while retaining the assumptions behind each comparison. The result is a theoretical calculation, not simulated collider data.

Change only g₄.

guides.title: Simulator: Higgs production from a top KK tower
guides.what: Compare the leading top-KK correction to Higgs production with finite-tower and resummed low-energy-theorem calculations under a stated domain policy.
steps: Select Higgs production in the Simulator model selector.
Start from the Carson–Okada reference and read its historical rate window.
Vary the KK scale, top mass or numerical cutoff separately.
Compare numerical truncation, the leading/resummed difference and the conditional allowed interval.
guides.read: The historical window reproduces a source benchmark; a custom window is a user scenario with no assigned confidence level. The numerical tail and the small-x expansion comparison do not quantify all physical theory uncertainty.
guides.purpose: Use this to study one isolated production-rate mechanism without treating it as a complete GHU signal calculation. The finite sum tests how many KK terms are needed, while the resummed comparison asks a different approximation question.

controls.name: KK scale and top mass
controls.meaning: Set the ratio x = m_t/M_KK governing this reference correction. Use the displayed units.
controls.try: Increase the KK scale with the top mass fixed.

controls.name: KK cutoff
controls.meaning: Sets how many terms enter the finite leading tower.
controls.try: Increase it while keeping the physical inputs fixed and read the tail bound.

controls.name: Reference or custom rate window
controls.meaning: Defines the interval against which the rate is compared.
controls.try: Read both window edges; do not interpret a custom window as a new experimental likelihood.

outputs.name: Leading and resummed rates
outputs.meaning: Two calculations with different approximation scope inside the same top-only reference.

outputs.name: Finite-tower tail bound
outputs.meaning: Bounds the omitted leading-sum contribution, not missing particles or higher-order physical effects.

outputs.name: Conditional scale interval
outputs.meaning: Intersects the chosen rate window with the laboratory policy x ≤ 0.2.

example.title: Separate truncation from approximation
steps: Use the historical reference inputs.
Increase the cutoff and inspect the finite-tower tail.
Compare the converged leading rate with the resummed rate.
Change the user window and observe that the conditional interval changes without changing the rate formula.
example.expect: A smaller numerical tail does not remove the difference between physical approximations.

formulas.meaning: The leading top-only reference rate from Carson–Okada under the stated spectrum and approximation.
The independently resummed determinant low-energy-theorem amplitude. Its square is not a full finite-mass loop calculation.

limits: The x ≤ 0.2 policy defines the displayed working domain; it does not promise a uniform physical accuracy.
Branching fractions and additional coloured particles are outside this mode.
The historical scale bound is not presented as a current global exclusion.

troubleshooting.symptom: The current rate or verdict is withheld.
troubleshooting.action: Check whether x exceeds the displayed domain policy.

troubleshooting.symptom: The finite sum converges but differs from the resummed result.
troubleshooting.action: Read the distinction between truncation of the leading sum and the small-x expansion within the low-energy theorem.

guides.title: Simulator: the 4D neutrino ring
guides.what: Explore light masses, active-current deficit and six heavy pairs in the supported four-dimensional neutrino-ring research model.
steps: Choose Neutrino ring and start from its default point.
Read whether calibration is enabled: it fixes two chosen light-sector targets.
Change one link, portal or Majorana input and inspect masses and active weights together.
Use the dedicated flavour, fixed-light-input and decay guides before interpreting those additional experiments.
guides.read: The calibration targets are supplied inputs, not predictions. Heavy centres, light masses and pair splittings use different displayed units. The CMS overlay is a conditional single-HNL reference comparison, not a full multi-state ring exclusion.
guides.purpose: Use this to study how a model can preserve selected light-sector quantities while changing its heavy states and interactions. This is a four-dimensional deconstructed ring at a fixed phase background, with explicitly stated leading-order approximations. It is separate from the five-dimensional builder.

controls.name: Scale f, link t/f and portals q, r
controls.meaning: Set the conserving mass structure. The scale is dimensionful; the link and portal ratios are dimensionless.
controls.try: Change one ratio at fixed f and read the heavy centres.

controls.name: Majorana inputs μA and μB
controls.meaning: Small symmetry-breaking mass entries displayed in keV.
controls.try: Vary μB with calibration enabled and compare light inputs with pair splittings.

controls.name: Calibration
controls.meaning: Solves for entries that reproduce the chosen 0.1 eV light mass and 10⁻⁴ deficit in the reference setup.

references.label: SU(7) certification: statements, assumptions and attribution

alphabet.body: A boundary condition on an orbifold is a representation of the space group Γ = Λ ⋊ Z_m, so the possible conditions are built out of Irr(Γ) — the letters. Part IX-A gets them by Möbius inversion over the fixed points of the rotation, with Clifford theory supplying the weights. Everything else on the orbifold page is derived from this list; nothing is entered.

weight.body: Its dimension. A letter of weight one is a diagonal boundary condition. A letter of weight above one is exactly a boundary condition that is not diagonal — which is why an alphabet with heavy letters cannot be read off a diagonal ansatz, and why the weights, not the number of letters, set the cost of enumerating a rank.

local-datum.body: At a cone point of order e, the eigenvalues of the isotropy element acting on the condition, recorded as multiplicities over the e-th roots of unity. It is local: it says what the condition looks like at that one fixed point and nothing about the rest of the orbifold.

class.body: Its tuple of local data, one entry per cone point. This is what any equivalence relation must preserve, so a proposed relation that moves one local datum is wrong, and the check costs seconds and does not need the classification to be finished.

fibre.body: All the boundary conditions carrying the same class. The classes are the fibres of a marginal map, which is why they are indexed by an affine semigroup rather than by a list. In the panels a cell of the lattice is a fibre: its footprint is the class count and its volume is the number of conditions.

cone.body: The fixed points of the rotation on the torus, each with the order of its isotropy group. The signature is the list of those orders, and it alone fixes the degree of the class count in the rank — before any condition is enumerated.

frobenius-schur.body: +1, 0 or −1: whether a letter is real, complex, or quaternionic. It is what decides how the SU alphabet merges into the SO and Sp ones — a complex letter pairs with its conjugate, a real one survives alone — so the three real forms are not three separate computations but one alphabet read three ways.

degree.body: The degree of polynomial growth of the class count under the classification hypotheses is e₁ − 1, where e₁ = 1 + Σ c(mᵢ), with c(m) = m−1 for SU and ⌊m/2⌋ for SO and Sp. This asymptotic degree is distinct from asserting that every exact finite-rank count is one polynomial without periodic terms.

hilbert-series.body: The counts are the Hilbert function of the semigroup, so the generating function is P(x) / ∏(1−x^w) over the letter weights. The point is that P terminates: that is checked here, not assumed, and once it does the counts at any rank come from the recurrence with nothing enumerated.

unbroken-group.body: The 4D gauge group a condition looks like it leaves unbroken, S(∏ U(n_ℓ)) for a weight-one alphabet. It is not an invariant of the class: conditions in one fibre — the same theory — can wear different apparent symmetries. That is why a survey that lists models by their apparent group double-counts.

smith-normal-form.body: How the fixed points are actually enumerated. They are M⁻¹Zʳ/Zʳ, a group of order |det M|, and the normal form walks exactly that many points. The naive box walks |det M|ʳ of them, which is the same answer at rank 2 and hopeless at rank 6 — where the heterotic orbifolds are.

crystallographic.term: why a matrix can be refused
crystallographic.body: An integer matrix of infinite order is not the rotation of any orbifold, so it is returned refused rather than classified. The same for a matrix whose characteristic polynomial is not a power of the m-th cyclotomic: that is outside the hypothesis of Part IX-A, and the machinery would answer with an empty alphabet and degree zero — which looks like an answer and is not one.

move.body: A rewriting that preserves the stated class data. Completeness is the stronger claim that a move set connects every member of every relevant fibre. The finite walk tests connectivity for the selected case; legitimate individual moves and success at one rank alone do not prove completeness at every rank.

affine-semigroup.body: The classes are the fibres of a marginal map, so they are indexed by a semigroup with one generator per letter of the alphabet. Naming that semigroup is mostly an exercise in attribution: over Z₂ it is a cut configuration with a literature and a published table of invariants, and the useful thing this page can do is stop you deriving it again.

wilson-line.body: The vacuum expectation value of the extra-dimensional gauge field, in units where a period is 1. In this family it is the electroweak hierarchy, because 1/R₅ = 2m_W/α — which is why a phase of order 10⁻³ and a scale of order tens of TeV are the same statement.

hosotani.body: A higher-dimensional gauge-field component can supply a four-dimensional Higgs zero mode. In the supported gauge-invariant setup its Wilson-line potential is generated radiatively. The phase can be calculated within a model, but dimensionful predictions still require the stated scale and coupling inputs; calibrating with measured m_W is not a prediction of that same input.

parities.body: Signs of a component at the orbifold fixed points, such as (+,+) or (+,−). In the ordinary untwisted interval problem, a (+,+) component admits a constant zero mode before Wilson backgrounds and additional mass terms. At a nontrivial vacuum the joint boundary problem must be evaluated; a parity table alone is not the complete physical spectrum.

zero-mode.body: A mode at the bottom of the compactification spectrum that is massless under the stated background and boundary problem. At the ordinary symmetric point its existence follows from the component parities. Wilson backgrounds, boundary masses and other interactions can change the massless content, so the chosen background must accompany the count.

kk-tower.body: The four-dimensional modes associated with an extra-dimensional field. In the simplest untwisted case masses are n/R, while boundary phases can shift the levels and boundary kinetic terms can change the spectral equation. A tower must retain its boundary conditions, phase convention and multiplicities; it does not by itself determine collider rates.

bulk-content.body: The list of representations living in the extra dimensions, each with its orbifold parities and a multiplicity. It is the input to everything — potential, spectrum, anomalies and scale are all functions of it.

brane.body: The ends of the interval, where the orbifold has its fixed points. Fields can live there as well as in the bulk, and that matters twice over: the anomaly of this class of models sits entirely on the fixed points, and brane fermions are what pay for unwanted zero modes.

local-group.term: the local group at a fixed point
local-group.body: At y = 0 the local group is the commutant of P₀; for diagonal blocks it is S(U(n₊₊ + n₊₋) × U(n₋₊ + n₋₋)). At y = πR it is the commutant of P₁. These local groups can differ, and the symmetric-point 4D group commutes with both. A local representation can split into several representations of that common subgroup.

boundary-mass.term: a boundary mass, and the rank test
boundary-mass.body: A Weyl fermion on a fixed point can pair with a bulk zero mode and give it a mass. In a fully left-handed convention the rule is one line: a mode in r_q pairs with a localised Weyl in r̄₋q — conjugate representation, opposite charge. What is easy to get wrong is the counting: with generic couplings the mass matrix has maximal rank, so what survives is |difference| in each class separately, and a count of exotics that skips the decomposition can declare a mass allowed that is not.

one-loop-potential.body: The effective Wilson-line potential obtained at one loop from the supported field content and compactification spectrum. Its phase-dependent part is finite in the stated protected setup. This does not quantify every higher-loop correction, boundary interaction or physical theory uncertainty, and an implemented potential still needs a justified normalization and field content.

alpha-min.body: The closed form locates a stationary branch within the small-phase expansion. It is compared with a numerical search of the Fourier potential; the two can differ. Neither the closed form nor a finite grid alone certifies the global vacuum.

chiral.body: Left- and right-handed fields in different representations — which is the point of orbifolding, and the reason the 4D theory can look like the Standard Model. It is also a gate: a chiral spectrum is inconsistent unless its gauge anomalies cancel.

anomaly-channel.body: A chiral spectrum has to have its gauge anomalies cancel, channel by channel — tedious, and where an arithmetic slip hides best. A non-zero entry is not a verdict of inconsistency: these models carry brane fields anyway, and a brane fermion conjugate to a zero mode contributes to the same channel with the opposite sign. So the ledger reports a bill, and says who can pay it.

blkt.body: An extra kinetic term localised on a fixed point. Turn it on and the Kaluza–Klein masses stop being n/R: they become the roots of a transcendental equation, sliding off the poles of the free summand, and the potential has to be built from those roots instead of written down.

boundary-condition.body: The choice of how the gauge group acts at each fixed point — for SU(N) on S¹/Z₂, the block sizes [p, q, r, s]. It is what breaks the group, and there are many of them, which is the first problem a model builder meets.

equivalence-class.term: when two boundary conditions are one theory
equivalence-class.body: Some boundary conditions are related by a gauge transformation, so they are the same theory wearing different clothes; only the class is physics. Two things follow: the apparent unbroken symmetry is not an invariant of the class — SU(5) with [2,0,0,3] looks like SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1) and [1,1,1,2] like SU(2)×U(1)³, and they are one theory — and a survey that does not quotient by this counts the same model over and over.

moments.body: Charge-weighted second and fourth moments describe the small-phase reduction of the implemented potential. The allowed arithmetic depends on the gauge seed: the published SU(7) seed gives odd 8D, whereas the candidate seed has even rungs. Read the seed and nondegeneracy conditions before using a stationary branch or a curvature verdict; moments do not generally determine the full potential.

rung.body: A quantized value of the curvature coordinate D in the stated moment reduction. Its parity and accessible values depend on the seed. Finite enumeration and counting statements require the stated additional coordinate or mass-window bounds. A search stopped by its computational budget has not proved that a rung contains no solution.

ceiling.body: An upper bound on the scale for the stated moment relaxation, gauge seed, coupling and Higgs-mass window. Rational or interval certificates establish that mathematical bound under those hypotheses. It need not be attained by an integer content and is not automatically a universal bound on full-potential global vacua or on a physically reconciled model.

reachable-set.body: Scales reached by the integer contents admitted in the stated inverse-design problem. They can form separated clusters rather than a continuous interval. A quoted gap must retain its seed, mass window, coupling and approximation; a plot or a budget-limited search alone is not a certificate that every intermediate scale is impossible.

certificate.body: Evidence for a precisely stated mathematical claim and its hypotheses: for example an arithmetic obstruction, a rational bound, or an interval proof for a fixed potential. The claim and domain travel with the certificate. A budget stop is undecided, and certifying an implemented formula does not prove its full physical applicability or scientific novelty.

vector-partition-function.body: The multiplet lattice with its congruence is a rational cone cut by an affine sublattice, so the count at fixed (A₄, 8D) is a vector partition function. A dynamic programme gives every count at once in milliseconds, where building the contents one at a time took about twenty-five minutes and ran out of budget.

same-potential.term: when two contents give one potential
same-potential.body: Part VII Theorem 3 gives an if-and-only-if equality criterion in five coordinates for the implemented potential family. Distinct multiplet contents can therefore give the same Wilson-line potential. Matching only selected local moments or plotted samples is weaker; equal potentials do not establish equality of all spectra, interactions or complete physical theories.

canonical-representative.body: A distinguished content among those with the same implemented potential, as defined in Part VII, equation (43). It provides a reproducible representative for that algebraic equality. It is not automatically a canonical representative of a complete physical theory: quantities not encoded by the potential can still differ.

selection-rule.body: Part III: one bit, arithmetic on three integers, says that half the torus is redundant — you never have to search it. The claim is testable by a computation that has never heard of Dynkin labels, which is what this page runs.

eta.body: The boundary-condition sign η = η₀η₁. Part V shows it rides on an index alone, so it is invisible to the Higgs potential exactly on Part IV's vanishing class.

eta-blindness.body: In the SU(4) projection and potential contribution studied in Parts IV–V, the stated vanishing-index class has no η-dependent response. Increasing its multiplicity does not create that sign-dependent difference. This does not mean its full potential contribution, spectrum or other physical effects vanish; compare full-potential and η-difference views separately.

k-invariant.body: m_h a / √F'' = 2.2456 g₄ in the registered convention. At fixed input m_h, F → λF changes K by λ^(−½). Invariance requires also recomputing m_h as √λ m_h. This compares the implied coupling; it does not establish stationarity or a global minimum. Part VI, open problem 3.

comb.body: The KK scale can only sit on teeth, spaced exactly in M² and not in M, with each rung's teeth stopping at its own ceiling. The spacing is arithmetic and carries nothing; the position carries the anchor residual and g₄. Confusing the two is how a screen becomes an accusation.

bill-in-eighths.body: The cost of an escape from the proton-decay obstruction, measured in the quantum of D. It is a ratio of integers, so no normalisation enters it — which is what lets it be quoted without an anchor.

rung-cube.body: The 64 ordered triples of lepton rungs, drawn. Its main diagonal is the family-universal line, where every A_j vanishes and the protection dies — so the failure set is a line, not a region, and the theorem is the geometry rather than a summary of it.

coloron.body: The colour-octet vector used in the laboratory’s stated dijet comparison. Its mass, width and coupling follow the localization and compactification assumptions of that model. A limit derived for another resonance, production mechanism or branching pattern cannot be transferred solely because a mass value matches.

recast.body: A published experimental bound re-expressed on this model's scale. The Δχ² teeth here are quoted from the published record, never re-derived — a near-miss re-derivation would put a number on the page that disagrees with the paper it claims to come from.

anchor.body: A published computation the instrument recomputes at load and shows as a chip, so the tool declares whether it currently reproduces an outside number before it shows you any of its own.

gauge-or-physics.body: A number the instrument computes about a boundary condition is only a statement about the theory if it survives replacing that boundary condition by a gauge-equivalent one. The dossier recomputes every line on every member of the class and tags it by what came back — so the tag is a measurement made on this render, never a list of which lines ought to be invariant. Most of the symmetric-point lines are not: the apparent unbroken group, the massless content and the anomaly ledger are read at θ = 0 of the representative you happen to be holding. The same three, read at the minimum, come back invariant — and that too is measured on the render.

sm-cell.body: Is SU(3)×SU(2)×U(1)_Y in the unbroken group, with massless pieces carrying Q, uᶜ, dᶜ, L and eᶜ at their hypercharges? Colour is a block of size three, weak isospin a block of size two, and Y is solved exactly in the blocks' U(1) generators on the pieces offered as each field — Part II's counting: K − 1 unknowns against one constraint per field. When the fields fix Y the embedding fixes sin²θ_W = tr T₃² / (tr T₃² + tr Y²), 3/8 for Georgi–Glashow's direction. It is read at the symmetric point nearest the vacuum, because the vacuum's job is to break SU(2)×U(1); the distance says whether the electroweak sector is light. What is not found is listed as missing — on SU(5) with P = diag(+,+,+,−,−) that is always Q and dᶜ, which the literature puts on the brane.

against-the-data.body: In the builder comparison, the vacuum supplies a dimensionless m_W R and the recorded measured W mass calibrates 1/R. This makes dimensionful quantities conditional on that anchor. A colour-octet reference limit applies only under its particle and localization assumptions, including colour in the bulk. Other modes use their own named datasets and hypotheses. Reference overlays, interval membership and statistical likelihoods are different comparisons; retain each source edition and input record.

at-the-minimum.body: Gauge the constant A_y away and the reflection about y = πR becomes P₁′ = W⁻¹P₁, with W the holonomy round the circle (Hosotani; Haba–Hosotani–Kawamura §2). A massless four-dimensional mode is a vector fixed by both P₀ and P₁′, so the content at the minimum is a joint eigenspace — linear algebra, not a parity table. When every phase is 0 or 1 it is the parity rule applied to a class-mate. A boundary face alone does not decide breaking: compare the surviving generators with those at θ = 0. The instrument reaches the count by two independent routes — the representation theory of the pairs the Wilson line rotates, and the explicit matrices — and the harness holds one to the other. The scalars are tree-level flat directions; the tolerance for "at an end" is 10⁻⁶.

separates-nothing.body: A line can be the same on every member of a class and also the same for every class, and then it distinguishes no theory from any other however stable it is — N₀ is one, and so is N. The two axes are independent and are measured separately: splitting within a class makes a line the frame's, and taking one value between classes makes it no verdict at all.

keyword-sweep.term: what a keyword sweep is worth
keyword-sweep.body: It turns a corpus into a shortlist, and that is all. A signal firing means “worth opening”; it is never quoted as a fact about a paper. The two are kept in separate columns here for exactly that reason.

measured-vs-read.body: Measured records describe the reproducible extraction or keyword sweep over the declared corpus. Read records are human-reviewed statements with a source page or equation. A PDF whose text extraction loses the needed glyphs is not evidence that its paper omits a formula; keep extraction failure separate from a negative literature finding.

tripod.body: For a finite abelian G, the group-based model on the claw tree with three leaves is a complete intersection iff |G| ≤ 3. The arithmetic settles orders five and up in one line, for every abelian group at once: |G|² − 6|G| + 6 ≤ 0. Order four passes the bound and is still not a complete intersection — Z₄ and Z₂×Z₂ are decided by exhaustion in Part IX-B §5, and a bound that is silent is reported as silent.

complete-intersection.body: Casanellas, Fernández-Sánchez and Michałek prove these varieties are complete intersections in a Zariski-open set. The question asked here is the global one, about the toric ideal itself, and the Z₄ tripod separates the two: local yes, global no. Quoting one for the other is the misreading this page exists to prevent.

anchor-verdicts.term: three verdicts, and the amber one is the output
anchor-verdicts.body: Green: the instrument returns what the paper prints. Amber: it does not — and the row names which of that paper's own equations agrees with which, and what moves as a result. Grey: outside this engine, said out loud, because a blank cell reads as a no and "we did not compute it" is not "it does not hold". A verdict that changes is what fails the build; a verdict that differs is what this page is for.

anchor-scope.term: what each row was read at
anchor-scope.body: Three of the four models are supersymmetric and this engine's one-loop potential is not, so their rows are parity linear algebra only — which boundary condition, which unbroken group, which zero modes — and never their dynamics. Kubo–Lim–Yamashita is not supersymmetric, which is why its potential, its vacuum and its Higgs mass can be anchored at all, and why it is the one where this engine can be wrong by a number.
